final4.thesis: XLV made its first weekly close above the old $169.71 ceiling, hitting an all-time high of $176.60 on the heaviest volume of 2026, and 13 of the 14 names we track rose. It moves almost independently of SPY (correlation -0.10) and trades on its own news: the intismeran Phase 3 win, a run of FDA approvals, and GILD's HIV-drug decision due Aug 27. That matters more to it than this week's PCE, NVDA and Warsh events. I'm wrong if a strong NVDA report plus a patient Warsh pull money back into tech and XLV falls below $169.71 (then the $167.09 20-day average), or if drug-pricing or tariff headlines hit pharma.

The oil premium now comes from a real supply cut, not headlines: Hormuz transits fell to 5 on Saturday and 0 on Sunday, the White House ruled out talks with Iran, and the weekly EIA stock build shrank to 4.4M barrels. XLE broke out to a 52-week high and moves against SPY (correlation -0.38), so it is the book's hedge if a hot PCE or a hawkish Warsh pushes the 10Y above 4.75%. I'm wrong if tankers start moving or talks restart: the war premium would drain out of WTI fast, and with RSI at 71.7 on light volume, XLE would fall back below its $63.46 breakout level.

This is a bet on the weak dollar and on metals, not on factory demand: the 56.0 PMI was driven by services, while manufacturing fell to a five-month low. The drivers are the dollar below 99, the flight into gold (up 5.6% to $4,624 after Treasury doubled its bond buybacks with the debt past $40T), Freeport's breakout on a forecast copper shortage, and steel tariff protection that survived when the Canada talks collapsed. XLB closed at a five-month high and led Friday's bounce. I'm wrong if a hawkish Warsh sends the dollar back above 100 and knocks Newmont (NEM) down from an RSI of 84.6, or if WTI goes above $90 and squeezes the chemical makers.

XLP finished flat in a week when WMT, its third-largest holding, fell 9.8%, because money moved into KO (at a 52-week high), PEP, GIS and CPB rather than leaving the sector. With a beta of about 0.52 it is the book's cushion if NVDA disappoints or the week turns risk-off, and the weak dollar helps the multinationals, but it is my weakest pick. I'm wrong if a cool PCE, a strong NVDA report and a patient Warsh spark a rally that leaves defensives behind, if the 10Y goes above 4.85% and hits bond-like staples, or if WMT keeps sliding after its miss and pulls COST down with it.

changes: No change to the four sectors or their order. Refinements: corrected the Materials case (factory index fell to a five-month low; the call rests on the dollar, gold, copper and steel tariff protection); named Staples the weakest pick and added a clear 'I'm wrong if' to every sector. Technology did not earn a swap and Real Estate stays out.
